title: p99/p95 tail latency deep dive with Cypherix LLC
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked through p95/p99 tail latency drivers for Cypherix's inference workload. Focus areas: KV cache behavior, continuous batching, quantization tradeoffs, streaming vs non-streaming for long generations, and network hops in VPC/on-prem setups. Action items include sharing benchmark spreadsheet, security docs, and scheduling a pilot to run a 24h tail-latency test in their VPC.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-21
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, Cypherix), Liam O'Connor (Lead ML Eng), Sofia Ruiz (Infra), Anil Mehta (Product)

Summary: quick deep dive on tail latency (p95/p99) for Cypherix inference; focus on runtime hotpaths, KV cache, batching, quantization, and network hops in VPC/on-prem.

00:00 Speaker 1: okay, um, let's get started. Thanks everyone for joining. Sam, I'll hand over to you.
00:18 Sam (Redwood AE): thanks, yeah hi all, appreciate you making time. Today Jordan and I wanted to go through the p95/p99 tail issues you saw in the benchmark you sent last week — thanks for the spreadsheet, that was super helpful. We'll cover causes and mitigations: caching, batching, quant, streaming, and also network hops if you're on VPC or planning on prem.
00:45 Jordan (Redwood SE): quick agenda, um, first a short primer on p95 vs p99 and why p99 is sensitive to outliers; then dive into runtime internals — KV cache warm/cold, continuous batching, and quantization behavior; finally network/infra stuff. We'll also show a couple of traces.
01:12 Maya (Cypherix): sounds good. Our big asks: we need p95 < 120ms and p99 < 400ms for short prompts (avg 40 tokens). For long generations (300+ tokens) we really care about median throughput but tails kill UX.
01:36 Jordan: got it. Just to align on definitions — for this call we'll use request latency as end-to-end from client send to first-token streaming and full-response latency for non-streaming. p95/p99 are computed over 5 minute windows for current dashboards.
02:05 Liam (Cypherix): the benchmark included both streaming and non-streaming numbers. We saw p95 for streaming is okay but p99 jumps a lot on certain times, especially when model updates and cache invalidations happen.
02:30 Jordan: yeah, that's common. A lot of p99 is caused by cache misses and cold KV cache behavior. Our runtime uses a KV cache for prefix tokens and sometimes the cache needs to be populated or misses due to model version pinning. When a single request triggers cache population that's a high-latency path.
02:58 Sam: also network hops — if your clients are routed cross-AZ or through a proxy, you can add 30-100ms per hop which shows up at p99. Sofia, can you describe your VPC layout?
03:20 Sofia (Cypherix): sure — we have multi-AZ with a NATGW in front of some subnets, and internal traffic crosses a transit gateway when we call external vendor APIs. We do plan to deploy Redwood Private in a peered VPC initially.
03:44 Jordan: transit gateways and NATs can add headroom. For p99 it's worth establishing VPC peering or private link to cut the extra hops — peering reduces jitter and TCP/TLS handshake variance. Also watch MTU mismatches and jumbo frames if you're seeing fragmentation.
04:10 Anil (Cypherix): quick Q — is KV cache stateful per GPU? If we scale out, do we lose cache warmness?
04:25 Jordan: good question. Our KV cache lives in the serving tier; depending on the config it can be partitioned per worker (per-GPU) or shared via a hot cache layer. Scaling up can increase cold-cache probability unless you use a shared cache or sticky routing. We recommend sticky routing or prefix caching at the load-balancer level for latency-sensitive workloads.
04:52 Speaker 1: (mumble) sticky routing, ok.
05:05 Jordan: another cause of tail latency is batching dynamics. If you use naive batching with a timer + size, some requests wait to fill a batch; continuous batching tries to balance throughput and latency by dynamically pulsing batch sizes. For p99, you want to avoid batching knobs that allow long wait timers. Smaller max batch size and tight timers reduce p99 but hurt throughput.
05:40 Liam: yes we saw the timer spike: when traffic dips, p99 went up because batches weren't filling. Could Redwood autoscaling help?
05:55 Jordan: autoscaling helps at throughput but isn't a silver bullet for p99. Two levers: lower batch wait time and enable dynamic batching to avoid inflating single-request latency. Also consider adaptive routing: route small short prompts to low-concurrency pools.
06:20 Sam: to add, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs — streaming sometimes reduces perceived p99 to first-token (you get output earlier), but tail for full generation could still be high for final tokens. For long outputs, streaming plus partial caching helps UX.
06:50 Maya: can you explain prefix caching more — we have many few-shot prompts with the same system prompt.
07:01 Jordan: prefix or KV cache stores attended keys/values for tokens in the prefix. If many requests reuse the same prefix (e.g., system prompt + few-shot examples), the runtime can reuse the KV cache and skip recomputing those tokens. That reduces compute and latency significantly. But cache TTL, eviction, and model-version mismatches cause misses. If you push a new model, caches invalidated — you'll see a p99 spike.
07:40 Liam: how big is the hit for a cache miss?
07:46 Jordan: depends on seq length. For a 40-token prefix on a 2B model on a single GPU, a cache miss could add 50–120ms; on larger models or CPU-backed paths it can be seconds. For the tail, if a single request populates caches for many tokens, it balloons.
08:10 Sam: also watch KV cache serialization when you cross process boundaries or use shared Redis-like caches — serialization/deserialization adds jitter. Our optimized path keeps KV in-memory co-located with the worker when low-latency is required.
08:35 Speaker 1: (background) mmhm.
08:50 Jordan: quantization — moving from fp16 to int8 can reduce latency by up to ~20–40% per token depending on kernel coverage. But quant sometimes impacts quality; we recommend running a small eval set for regression. Also quant can change memory access patterns and tail behavior; int8 kernels can be faster but occasionally trigger different kernel dispatch paths which show up in p99 if not profiled.
09:25 Maya: we heard int8 gives jittery perf on certain GPUs due to mixed precision fallbacks, is that a Redwood thing?
09:36 Jordan: not Redwood-specific — it's GPU and kernel-compiler specific. The runtime picks kernels based on architecture and model ops. We provide profiles and a recommended quantization profile per model/hardware to minimize regressions.
09:58 Liam: are there any tradeoffs for streaming vs running non-streamed then sending the full response?
10:10 Jordan: streaming reduces time-to-first-byte; it lets you emit partial tokens as they're produced. For p99 of first-token latency streaming helps a lot, because you don't wait for full decode. For p99 of full-response however, streaming doesn't fix expensive finalization steps (e.g., long decode loops, sampling, or slow kernel dispatch). Also network-level retries can cause duplicate partial streams — we generally recommend streaming for interactive UX and non-streaming for batch workloads.
10:48 Sam: an operational note — instrument both first-byte and last-byte latencies in your monitoring. Use histograms with exponential buckets and also capture per-request trace ids so you can correlate spikes with infra events.
11:12 Jordan: we'll share a sample histogram chart and example percentile calculation. Also look at p50/p90/p95/p99 across different workload slices (seq length, prompt type, model variant).
11:30 Maya: about model variants — we sometimes fall back to smaller models during load; does that mitigate tail?
11:40 Jordan: yes routing to smaller model variants lowers latency and reduces p99, but can reduce quality. Automatic fallback policies can be tuned by route: if latency SLO breached then switch to compatible variant. We recommend validating output quality of fallback variants first.
11:58 Liam: we saw an odd spike correlated with a control-plane rollout — is there any coupling there?
12:06 Jordan: possible. If config changes trigger worker restarts, you get cold-workers which cause cache losses and compaction/GC in the runtime. Try to use rolling updates with warm standby and notify workload owners before big rollouts.
12:28 Sam: I want to walk through a couple of sample traces Jordan pulled from your run.
12:34 Jordan: trace 1 — 00:00:12 shows a 780ms tail where request waited 300ms in a pre-batch timer, then 120ms for a cache population step and 350ms for a network retry to metadata service. So it was a combined effect: batching timer + cache miss + external call.
13:05 Maya: that external metadata call is our user-profiles service — we do a sync call to enrich inputs, that's probably the network part.
13:15 Jordan: yep moving that enrichment earlier or caching the result can cut 100–300ms off those tails. Also decouple external calls from the critical path if possible.
13:36 Speaker 1: (crosstalk) right.
13:50 Jordan: trace 2 — 00:23:19 long-run generation: high CPU steal on the host was present and NVLink thrashing on a multi-GPU node led to a 1s tail. That's rarer but shows up in on-prem or shared noisy neighbors.
14:12 Sofia: for on-prem we're planning multi-tenant GPU boxes with worker pinning; what best practices for reducing cross-tenant noise?
14:25 Jordan: dedicate GPUs for latency-critical pools, use cgroups to cap CPU interference, isolate nvlink traffic patterns, and prefer single-tenant or strict tenant isolation for p99-sensitive workloads.
14:46 Sam: network peering specifics — for VPC peering vs private link: peering is lower-latency but requires more network setup; private link gives better security but may route through additional proxies and add jitter. For strict p99 you want as few intermediaries as possible.
15:14 Anil: curious about TLS handshake overhead — we terminate TLS at the infra edge and forward plaintext internally; is that recommended?
15:26 Jordan: terminating TLS at the edge reduces CPU work on worker nodes; but ensure you still have mTLS or a secure internal network. TLS handshake cost shows up on each connection; keep long-lived connections or use HTTP/2 multiplexing to amortize.
15:48 Liam: measuring jitter — we saw more variance at 03:00 UTC. Any tips to correlate?
15:56 Jordan: correlate with infra jobs: backups, EBS snapshots, cron jobs that spike I/O. Also capture host-level metrics (cpu steal, iowait) and packet drops. We'll give you a checklist to correlate host/az events with p99 spikes.
16:22 Sam: let's talk quantization a bit more — int8 kernels differ by vendor; Redwood's compilation picks the best kernel set per hardware but you should run a small perf/quality matrix. We can automate the search in Redwood Optimize; Jordan can run a quick study for your model & target hardware.
16:50 Jordan: example: on Ampere A100 int8 gives 30% step-down in token latency on certain kernels; on older GPUs the benefit is smaller and sometimes negative due to fallback. We'll provide recommended profiles per GPU.
17:10 Maya: how do we isolate p99 issues to network vs runtime vs model?
17:18 Jordan: trace all the way: client-side timestamp, LB ingress timestamp, worker start/finish, cache hit/miss logs, kernel dispatch times, and network hops. Use trace ids and tag each span with AZ/host/worker-id. We'll give a sample tracing layout.
17:44 Sam: I'll also note that continuous batching combined with prefix caching often gives best unit economics while keeping tail latencies acceptable. But it needs careful tuning and sticky routing.
18:05 Liam: for our workload (mix of short interactive and long batch), what's a recommended split?
18:12 Jordan: route short interactive to a dedicated low-concurrency pool with small batch timers and streaming enabled. Route long batch to high-throughput pools with larger batches but keep an autoscaling rule so that you don't queue endlessly. Use sampling to compute tail percentiles per pool.
18:36 Jordan: a few operational tips: 1) sample 1% of requests for full traces, 2) keep rolling histograms for 1m/5m/1h windows, 3) emit p99 on both first-byte and full-response, 4) capture cache hit ratios by endpoint.
19:02 Maya: are there Redwood features that help with automatic fallback when p99 is breached?
19:10 Sam: yes — Redwood routing supports policy-based fallbacks: route by latency SLO, cost tier, or region. You can specify canaries and automatic fallback to compatible variants. Also e.g., if Dedicated pool overloaded, route to hosted or a smaller quantized variant.
19:32 Liam: do you have examples of safe fallback policies?
19:38 Jordan: we usually do: if p99_first_byte > 1.5x target for 1m, route 25% of traffic to fallback for 5 mins and measure quality delta; if acceptable, ramp. Always pre-validate fallback outputs.
19:58 Anil: about model updates — is rolling update support transparent for cache?
20:05 Jordan: rolling updates are supported but a new model version invalidates KV caches by design if the weights change. We support warm-up steps: pre-seeding cache with follow-up requests, or using blue/green model rollout with pinned traffic to avoid mass invalidations.
20:32 Jordan: another important point — serialization and RPC overhead if you use remote KV store (like Redis) for cache will add jitter; prefer in-memory local cache for p99-sensitive endpoints.
20:50 Speaker 1: hmm ok.
21:02 Jordan: sample numbers from our internal benchmark: baseline p50/p95/p99 for short prompts on Redwood Dedicated with optimized kernels and KV warm: 45ms / 95ms / 210ms. With cold KV and naive batching: 55ms / 180ms / 750ms. With int8 quantization and optimized batching: 35ms / 80ms / 160ms (but measure quality).
21:36 Maya: useful. Can you share the benchmark harness?
21:40 Sam: yes will share that sheet.
21:47 Jordan: on network hops we often see per-hop jitter of 5–30ms on cloud; cross-AZ adds 10–50ms. Inconsistent MTU or packet loss makes TCP retransmits show up big at p99.
22:08 Liam: what about TLS session reuse?
22:12 Jordan: reuse sessions and keep connections warm with HTTP/2. For serverless-like short-lived connections, handshake cost is non-trivial.
22:28 Sam: let's do a short checklist for immediate mitigations: 1) enable sticky routing for critical endpoints, 2) tune batch timers (lower for short prompts), 3) enable in-memory KV cache co-located with worker, 4) run quantization evals on a small eval set, 5) move external enrichments off the critical path, 6) consider VPC peering or private link to reduce network hops.
23:05 Maya: we can action most of these. For on-prem long-term, we want deterministic p99 — what's the path there?
23:16 Jordan: on-prem best practices: dedicated racks for latency-sensitive pools, PCIe/NVLink topology that minimizes cross-GPU hops, isolate infra jobs, and use pinned workers + local KV caches. Also ensure low-latency fabric (roce/infiniband) if you do model parallelism.
23:45 Sam: question — what's your traffic shape, Maya? You shared some numbers but any diurnal or bursty patterns?
23:52 Maya: peak around 14:00 UTC and we have unpredictable bursts when customers run batch exports.
24:02 Jordan: bursts are where autoscaling + dynamic routing help. Also batch shaping — move heavy batch jobs to off-peak windows and give them dedicated queues.
24:20 Liam: on KV cache TTLs — any rules of thumb?
24:25 Jordan: TTL depends on prefix reuse. For relatively static system prompts, long TTLs (hours) are fine. For user-specific prefixes shorter TTLs or per-user caches are better. But remember memory tradeoffs.
24:40 Sam: I'm going to open the shared benchmark and point at the rows that show cold vs warm behavior...
24:48 [screen share; some crosstalk about numbers, not all transcribed clearly]
25:20 Jordan: example mitigation sequence for a p99 event: 1) detect spike in p99_first_byte, 2) query recent traces to identify cache misses/external calls/queue wait, 3) if external calls present, short circuit or cache them; if cache misses, warm caches or redirect traffic to warmed pool, 4) if infra cause, scale out or failover to hosted.
26:02 Maya: can Redwood do a temporary fallback to hosted while we debug?
26:08 Sam: yes we can route some traffic to Redwood Hosted as a safety valve; we'd need to align on data residency and security configs.
26:22 Anil: any security concerns with peering vs hosted?
26:28 Sam: peering keeps traffic in your VPC and is typically preferred for strict security; hosted requires careful contract and encryption in transit plus optionally bring-your-own-key. We'll share security docs.
26:44 Jordan: one more runtime detail — KV cache warmup: for blue/green deploys you can play back a sample of saved prefix requests to warm caches before switching traffic. That reduces p99 spike on deploy.
27:05 Liam: interesting, can Redwood simulate a warmup?
27:11 Jordan: yes we have tooling to pre-seed caches with representative prefixes. We'll include a small script.
27:25 Maya: what's the impact of model size? We're considering moving from 7B to 13B family — how will that change tail behavior?
27:33 Jordan: larger models increase per-token latency and memory pressure which often increases p99 sensitivity. If you go from 7B to 13B you may see 1.5–2x token latency; heavier models also raise cache memory use and eviction pressure, so you may need larger caches or more aggressive routing rules. Quantization helps but test quality.
27:58 Speaker 1: ok.
28:10 Jordan: to summarize technical mitigations: sticky routing, in-memory co-located KV cache, continuous/dynamic batching with tight timers for interactive pools, streaming for first-byte improvements, careful quantization and fallback policies, and network simplification (peering/private-link).
28:40 Sam: we'll send the benchmark sheet and an initial pilot plan. Any further questions?
29:00 Maya: one more on observability — can you expose per-request kernel timings?
29:06 Jordan: we can expose aggregated kernel timings and some sampled per-request spans; full low-level kernel timings are often vendor-provided, but we surface high-level dispatch/queue/compute spans.
29:22 Liam: ok great.
29:30 [the call continues with a couple of clarifying questions and scheduling notes; not all lines transcribed]
30:05 Sam: final recap — action items and next steps (see shared doc). We'll set up the pilot and share the checklist. Thanks all.
30:20 Maya: thanks, appreciate it.

Notes on transcription: some audio dropouts around 00:13 and 25:00; speaker labels may be approximate.
notes: Audio had some dropouts early and late; speaker labels approximate. Customer wants p95 < 120ms and p99 < 400ms for short prompts. Agreed pilot and to share artifacts.
